TL;DR What is […] The post Deep Principle Releases Hydrogen-1.0: A 753B Open-Weight Model for Scientific Discovery appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Deep Principle has released Hydrogen-1.0 , an open-weight scientific model for chemistry, materials science and life sciences. It is built by post-training Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 on domain data, laboratory records and agent discovery trajectories. For developers, it offers open weights that report a FrontierScience-Research win over GPT-6-Astra. The weights ship under the MIT License. TL;DR Size: 753B parameters (MoE, ~40B active per the GLM-5.3 base), 1M-token context, 128K max output. Runs on: 8 GPUs with SGLang (tested); NVFP4 for NVIDIA B200/B300, MXFP4 for AMD MI350X/MI355X. Performance: Beats GPT-6-Astra on FrontierScience-Research; roughly matches Kimi-K3 on GPQA-Diamond. Best: 38.3% on FrontierScience-Research vs 33.3% for GPT-6-Astra (self-reported). Worst: Trails GPT-6-Astra (max thinking) by 3.33 points on NMR structure elucidation. What is Hydrogen-1.0? Hydrogen-1.0 is a scientific research assistant model from Deep Principle, a Hangzhou-based AI-for-materials company. The model card describes it as a GLM-5.3 derivative for scientific problem solving. It targets question framing, experiment planning, results analysis and open-ended discovery. Deep Principle team states that proprietary models produced recent AI science results, but their discovery capabilities are not open. Hydrogen-1.0 is its attempt at a reproducible, inspectable alternative. How was Hydrogen-1.0 trained? The pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). Data comes from 4 sources: Domain knowledge: chemistry, materials science and life sciences data. Research scenarios: task-specific feedback from Deep Principle scientists. Laboratory records: full-cycle electronic lab notebook records captured through Mira . Discovery trajectories: sequences of choices and feedback, including failed attempts. Infrastructure builds on Megatron and SGLang across NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm. The team keeps dynamic sparse attention causal across context-parallel shards. Muon optimizer state is moved between CPU, GPU and disk per backend. RL uses resumable rollouts, and each token keeps its original behavior log-probability for importance correction. A layout adapter converts training checkpoints into BF16 and 128×128 blockwise FP8 inference weights. Full datasets and recipes are not released. How does Hydrogen-1.0 perform on benchmarks? On public benchmarks, Deep Principle reports Hydrogen-1.0 outperforms GPT-6-Astra on FrontierScience-Research. The tweet thread from one of the founders’ report 93.0% on GPQA-Diamond. That improves on GLM-5.3 and roughly matches Kimi-K3, per the blog. Internal research-task evals compare it with GPT-6-Astra at maximum thinking: Scientific computing: Hydrogen-1.0 leads by 5.13 percentage points. Forward reaction prediction: Hydrogen-1.0 leads by 4.76 percentage points. NMR structure elucidation: GPT-6-Astra leads by 3.33 points. In transition metal complex design, models chased a larger HOMO-LUMO gap over 5 rounds. By round 5, Hydrogen-1.0 reached a mean best-so-far gap of 4.318 eV. GPT-6-Astra reached 3.689 eV and Kimi-K3 reached 3.353 eV. On 117 experiment-planning questions, Hydrogen-1.0 scored above Kimi-K3. GPT-6-Astra and Opus-5.5 were excluded after refusing more than 50% of requests. What can it do in a real lab workflow? The technical post shows 4 demos . Hydrogen-1.0 writes Python to build a polyethylene melt and runs GROMACS. It detects a topology error, repairs it, and analyzes the corrected 40 ns trajectory. It grows an Ireland-Claisen reaction network of 27 structures through 30 plausible reactions. It ranks 7 candidate monoformylation products of 2-bromonaphthalene from a 1H NMR trace. It also writes a JSON protocol for a 12-vial Suzuki coupling study. A virtual lab compilation step catches an aspiration without a fresh tip before execution. How do you deploy Hydrogen-1.0? Weights are on Hugging Face and ModelScope . Deep Principle team tested BF16 serving with SGLang on 8 GPUs using tensor parallelism of 8. NVFP4 targets NVIDIA B200 and B300. MXFP4 targets AMD Instinct MI350X and MI355X. The server exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with a reasoning_effort setting. The post The Letter Company Releases Letterpress-1: A Coding Agent Built for Growth Engineering appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The Letter Company has released the beta of Letterpress-1 , a coding agent, harness and IDE for growth engineering. The Letterpress-1 coding agent reads a website and its market, then decides what should exist. It builds the change in a sandbox and opens a pull request with a live preview. TL;DR Size: Letter team says it combines frontier models with fine-tuned small models; names and sizes are not disclosed. Runs on: Letter’s hosted platform against your git repository. No local GPU needed. Setup takes under 5 minutes, per Letter. Performance: No public benchmark. Letter shows 1 self-reported, side-by-side page build against Codex. Best: 760 tools exposed through 1 registry over MCP, REST and CLI. Worst: No measurable eval; entry plan is $100/month with overage at 5x the list rate. What is Letterpress-1? Letterpress-1 is a growth engineering agent from The Letter Company. It turns site and market signals into pull requests. The letter company team argues that websites, unlike apps, react to outside forces. These include agent behavior, Google rankings, human visits and competitor activity . General coding agents were built to scale codebases, not to act on those signals. The agent is aimed at teams that host their marketing site in git. It is proactive: it suggests the next thing to build. Examples include de-anonymization, landing pages, warmed emails, blog automation and agent telemetry. How does Letterpress-1 work? Letterpress-1 runs in 3 modes : Build: create a page or feature from a prompt, with brand copy and visuals kept consistent. Plan: pick a goal and get a build plan of growth actions. Fix: find site issues and dispatch pull requests to fix them. Every change follows the same loop. The agent reads the site, plans and builds in a sandbox. It reviews its own change, then opens a pull request. Each change returns a preview link of your own site . Nothing lands until you choose a preview, a pull request, or a merge after checks pass. Letter team lists 6 surfaces. These are the web platform, a Slack app, the letterpress CLI and a website portal. A standalone app and your own agent round out the list. The in-site IDE works on a live page. Press ⌘L, edit text where you see it, and a pull request follows. Showcase examples also cover A/B tests from live edits. For developers, agents.md documents an MCP server at app.letterstory.com/api/mcp with OAuth. The MCP manifest, OpenAPI spec and API reference form 1 registry of 760 tools. Claude Code, Codex or any MCP-capable agent can call the same functions the app uses. What are Proofs, Simulations, Benches and Phantoms? The launch post highlights 4 primitives aimed at winning over AI agents as buyers: Proofs: signed evidence of customer success, built from telemetry and billing data, for agent visitors. Simulations: mirror versions of your API or MCP with simulated data, so agents can try before buying. Benches: self-hosted, reproducible benchmark apps with open-source code and independent governance. Phantoms: independent, autonomous blogs used to sandbox growth strategies. The site adds more: Kernels, Letterbases, Visitors and Mailers. Then it watches competitor sitemaps and flag new pages. Letter team positions these as replacements for tools like G2, Semrush, Profound, RB2B and Instantly.
